newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson raises Great Western bid, topping Washington.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson raises Great Western bid, topping Washington.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. Monday raised the stakes in the takeover battle for California thrift Great Western Financial Corp., topping Washington Mutual Savings Bank's $6.6 billion proposal by $400 million.
Ahmanson, the nation's biggest savings and loan, had previously offered $6.1 billion for Great Western, but Washington Mutual made its higher bid -- which Great Western accepted -- on March 6.
Ahmanson's latest salvo puts pressure on Washington Mutual Savings Inc. to follow suit.

"On a per dollar basis, it (Ahmanson) is a more attractive bid at this point and I imagine the onus is on Washington Mutual to make an improved offer," said Leslie Nelkin, an analyst with Furhman Selz.
Washington Mutual said it was not considering raising its offer and was confident its agreement with Great Western would prevail.

"Ahmanson's hostile actions do not alter the conclusion the Washington Mutual/Great Western combination will provide a stronger more finanically sound company in terms of tangible capital, credit quality and potential earnings power," a Washington Mutual spokesman said.

"Under our merger agreement, our transaction is to be considered by the shareholders at the earliest possible date and we're confident they'll approve the Great Western/Washington Mutual combination."
The spokesman said no date has yet been set for a shareholder vote on the deal.

Ahmanson said that based on the closing price of the shares of Washington Mutual and Ahmanson Friday, its improved offer provides a premium of about $3 a share over the implied value of the Washington Mutual proposal.
Ahmanson stock fell 50 cents to $39.75 and Great Western lost 25 cents to $45.25, both on the New York Stock Exchange, while Washington Mutual stock closed up 75 cents at $51.125 on Nasdaq.
Ahmanson, based in Irwindale, Calif., said its latest offer uses a floating exchange ratio for Great Western common shares linked to the market price for Ahmanson common shares.
Great Western stockholders would now receive, tax free, not less than 1.10 and not more than 1.20 common shares of Ahmanson for each common share of Great Western.
Ahmanson's previous offer, announced on Feb. 18, provided an exchange ratio of 1.05 Ahmanson common shares for each Great Western common share.
Based on the closing price of its stock on March 14, Ahmanson said, its latest exchange ratio is 1.20, worth $48.30 for each Great Western common share.
Ahmanson Chairman Charles Rinehart said he was confident that "we can responsibly assume an additional $100 million in merger benefits through our combination" with Great Western.
"We believe that this is a proposal that Washington Mutual cannot match without increasing its own shareholders' dilution to what must be an unacceptable level," he said.
Ahmanson said cost savings from the merger would be up by at least $50 million to $454 million. The company said it expects at least $50 million in revenue enhancements.

Analysts said the revised projections by Ahmanson were credible. Ahmanson has criticised Washington Mutual for what it considers to be overzealous projections. Several analysts have agreed with Ahmanson.
"While Ahmanson has added revenue enhancements, its original assumptions are still reasonable," said Nelkin.

Ahmanson executives said many of its newest assumptions were based on information released during Washington Mutual's presentations. Washington Mutual plans to meet with investors this week to outline its deal.

Many analysts preferred Ahmanson's offer due to its greater overlap with Great Western, which provides more cost savings. But other analysts said they had a lot of confidence in the ability of Washington Mutual to execute on its promises due to the company's proven track record with acquisitions.
Rinehart urged Great Western to provide Ahmanson with nonpublic information which it had given to Washington Mutual, and to hold talks on a definitive merger pact immediately.
Ahmanson, with assets of nearly $50 billion, owns Home Savings of America.
